notes: Same paper. CYP82AR homolog from L. officinale. Substrate=deoxyshikonin confirmed; which product (shikonin vs alkannin) requires full text.

Paper 1 (Humphreys 1999, PNAS): recombinant F5H in yeast shows Km for coniferaldehyde and coniferyl alcohol is 3 orders of magnitude lower than for ferulate, redefining preferred substrates. Paper 2 (Meyer 1998, PNAS): originally characterized as ferulate-5-hydroxylase. Conflict: newer 1999 paper shows ferulic acid is a poor substrate; preferred substrates are coniferaldehyde and coniferyl alcohol. Paper 3 (Weng 2012, Science) references CYP84A1 as lignin-biosynthetic ancestor without adding new substrate data. Preferred paper: Humphreys 1999 (newer, biochemically more detailed).

Abstract explicitly identifies CYP84A3 (LsM88) as coniferyl aldehyde 5-hydroxylase (CAld5H). kcat/Km for coniferyl aldehyde is ~140-fold higher than for ferulate; ferulate 5-hydroxylation abolished in presence of coniferyl aldehyde. Coniferyl alcohol not a substrate.

Abstract states CYP84A4 generates a catechol-substituted substrate for AtLigB in arabidopyrone biosynthesis, and that it is derived from phenylalanine via early phenylpropanoid metabolism. The specific substrate of CYP84A4 is not named in the abstract. Full text required to identify the direct substrate.

Abstract describes next-generation sequencing and characterization of CYP719A23/A24 (not CYP84A52) in podophyllotoxin biosynthesis. CYP84A52 is mentioned in the title as a sequenced candidate but its function is not addressed in the abstract. Full text required. [PARTIAL FROM FULLTEXT] Paper characterizes CYP719A23 (P. hexandrum) and CYP719A24 (P. peltatum) converting (-)-matairesinol to (-)-pluviatolide via methylenedioxy bridge formation. CYP84A52 is not individually named in the extracted abstract-level text. CYP84 family is typically involved in phenylpropanoid/lignan metabolism. The specific substrate-product pair for CYP84A52 cannot be confirmed from the available text; assignment to matairesinol/pluviatolide area is based on pathway context only.
No abstract available. Title indicates this is a rice ferulate-5-hydroxylase (CYP84 family), suggesting substrate=ferulate by analogy, but no biochemical confirmation extractable. Full text required.
Same paper as OsF5HL1, no abstract. Title indicates rice ferulate-5-hydroxylase gene. No biochemical confirmation available from abstract. Full text required.
No abstract available. Title indicates ferulate-5-hydroxylase from water chestnut. Substrate=ferulate inferred from gene name only; no biochemical confirmation from abstract. Full text required.

No abstract available. Title indicates ferrate-5-hydroxylase/coniferaldehyde 5-hydroxylase from Populus, suggesting dual substrate activity (ferulate and coniferaldehyde). No biochemical confirmation from abstract alone. Full text required.

reaction_type: oxidative modification of chlorophyll catabolites (dioxobilin formation)
notes: Abstract explicitly states CYP89A9 uses FCCs as substrates and produces fluorescent DCCs, confirmed by recombinant enzyme assay. FCCs originate as cytosolic intermediates from chloroplast export. Fluorescent DCCs then isomerize to NDCCs in vacuole.

reaction_type: oxidative rearrangement (ORA) and aromatic ring oxygenation
notes: Abstract explicitly states recombinant CYP92B14 converts (+)-sesamin to (+)-sesamolin via oxidative rearrangement (ORA) of alpha-oxy-substituted aryl group, and also generates (+)-sesaminol via direct aromatic ring oxygenation. Both products confirmed.

Abstract describes pathway reconstitution in N. benthamiana using metabolomic/transcriptomic approach. The function field explicitly states AsBX4 converts 3-hydroxyindolin-2-one to HBOA, consistent with BX4 function in the BXD pathway. However, the abstract does not directly name this substrate/product pair; it mentions evolutionarily unrelated P450s recruited to the pathway. Substrate assigned from function field + pathway logic. Full text recommended to confirm biochemical activity directly. [QC REJECTED: substrate not supported by abstract]

Same paper as AsBX4. Function field states LgBX4 converts 3-hydroxyindolin-2-one to HBOA (same as AsBX4), representing independent evolution of BXD biosynthesis in L. galeobdolon. Abstract confirms a P450 was recruited to the BXD pathway in this eudicot. Substrate assigned from function field + pathway context; full text recommended for direct biochemical confirmation.

Abstract characterizes BXD pathways in A. squarrosa and L. galeobdolon using FMO enzymes, not P450s. Mentions 'evolutionarily unrelated cytochrome P450s' recruited into eudicot BXD pathways but does not name CYP92A46 or its substrate explicitly. Function field (3-hydroxyindolin-2-one → HBOA) cannot be confirmed from abstract text alone. [UPDATED FROM FULLTEXT] CYP92A46 is the Scoparia dulcis functional equivalent of maize ZmBX4. Catalyzes hydroxylation of 3HI2O and subsequent ring expansion to produce HBOA. This is the BX4-equivalent step in the independently evolved BXD pathway of eudicots. CYP92A46 name not found in extracted text but function is established via DB annotation and paper context showing eudicot BX4-equivalent CYPs perform this ring expansion. [QC REJECTED: substrate not supported by abstract]

Same PNAS 2023 abstract as entry 460. Abstract does not name Wr BX4 or its substrate explicitly. Accession OQ921367 given but substrate assignment requires full text. [UPDATED FROM FULLTEXT] Wrightia religiosa BX4 (Apocynaceae) is a cytochrome P450 with BX4-equivalent function: converts 3HI2O to HBOA via hydroxylation and ring expansion. Part of independently evolved BXD pathway in eudicots. Paper (PNAS 2023) establishes that BXD biosynthesis arose independently at least three times in the plant kingdom. Consistent with DB function annotation.

Same PNAS 2023 abstract as entries 460–461. Abstract does not name Ai BX4 or its substrate explicitly. Accession OQ921369 given but substrate assignment requires full text. [UPDATED FROM FULLTEXT] Acanthus ilicifolius BX4 (Acanthaceae) is a P450 with BX4-equivalent function: converts 3HI2O to HBOA. Independently evolved eudicot BXD pathway enzyme. Same paper and reconstitution platform as Wr BX4 and CYP92A46. DB function annotation confirmed by paper context.

Abstract explicitly states CYP93A1 encodes dihydroxypterocarpan 6a-hydroxylase (D6aH), confirmed by NADPH dependency, stereoselectivity, and substrate affinity assays with recombinant protein in yeast. First isoflavonoid-specific CYP characterized at molecular level.

First paper (FEBS Lett 1998) explicitly demonstrates CYP93B1 (CYP Ge-5) converts (2S)-liquiritigenin to licodione and (2S)-naringenin to 2-hydroxynaringenin in insect-cell microsomes, and converts eriodictyol to luteolin in yeast. Second paper confirms flavone synthase II identity for CYP93B subfamily.

Abstract explicitly states yeast microsomes expressing CYP93B2 catalysed direct formation of [14C]-flavones from [14C]-flavanones. Specific flavanone substrates not named individually in abstract; full text would specify naringenin/eriodictyol. First functional FNS II cDNA reported from any species.

Abstract names AFNS2 from snapdragon (Antirrhinum majus) as CYP93B3, identified as flavone synthase II converting flavanones to flavones via 2-hydroxyflavanones. Specific substrates (e.g., naringenin) not stated individually in abstract.
Abstract names TFNS5 from torenia as CYP93B4 (=TFNS5), identified as flavone synthase II. Same paper as CYP93B3; specific substrates not stated individually in abstract.

reaction_type: flavanone to flavone conversion (flavone synthase II)
notes: Abstract explicitly states recombinant CYP93B6 expressed in yeast converted flavanones to flavones with measured Km values of 8.8–11.9 µM. Specific flavanone substrates (naringenin, eriodictyol, liquiritigenin) expected from family but not individually named in abstract.

Abstract describes MtFNSII-1 and MtFNSII-2 from M. truncatula (likely CYP93B10 and CYP93B11 respectively, per database accession numbers). MtFNSII converts flavanones to 2-hydroxyflavanones (not directly to flavones as in Gerbera). Abstract does not explicitly assign CYP93B10 vs CYP93B11 to MtFNSII-1 vs MtFNSII-2; full text needed for definitive assignment.

Same paper as CYP93B10. Abstract discusses MtFNSII-1 and MtFNSII-2; CYP93B11 is the second paralog. Specific accession-to-gene-name mapping not stated in abstract. Both convert flavanones to 2-hydroxyflavanones. Full text needed to distinguish CYP93B10 vs CYP93B11 substrate preferences.

Title-only entry: 'Heterologous Expression of Two Gentian Cytochrome P450 Genes can Modulate the Intensity of Flower Pigmentation in Transgenic Tobacco Plants'. No abstract available. Substrate cannot be determined from title alone.

reaction_type: flavanone to flavone direct conversion (flavone synthase II)
notes: Abstract explicitly demonstrates direct conversion: liquiritigenin → DHF, naringenin → apigenin, eriodictyol → luteolin by CYP93B16 expressed in yeast. Reaction is stereoselective, preferring (S)-enantiomers. Detailed biochemical characterization performed.

reaction_type: flavone synthase II (FNSII) - oxidative dehydrogenation/aromatization of flavanone
notes: Abstract describes a CYP82 family enzyme (flavone-6-hydroxylase) from sweet basil trichomes — not CYP93B23. The abstract does not name CYP93B23. The paper's focus is on a CYP82 P450 hydroxylating position 6 of 7-O-methylated apigenin, and a 2-oxoglutarate-dependent demethylase. CYP93B23 substrate requires full text consultation. [UPDATED FROM FULLTEXT] CYP93B23 is the Ocimum basilicum FNSII. It is cited as the reference FNSII in the Scutellaria paper (entry 474). The basil flavone paper (doi:10.1074/jbc.M112.420448) characterizes a CYP82D enzyme (not CYP93B23) as the flavone-6-hydroxylase acting on 7-O-methylated flavones; CYP93B23 itself catalyzes the upstream FNSII step converting (2S)-flavanones to flavones. Standard FNSII reaction: (2S)-naringenin -> apigenin; (2S)-eriodictyol -> luteolin.

products: flavones (apigenin from naringenin; chrysin from pinocembrin; luteolin from eriodictyol)
notes: Abstract describes FNSII-1 (broad flavanone specificity) and FNSII-2 (specific for pinocembrin) from S. baicalensis roots. Accession KT963453 is CYP93B24, but the abstract does not state which accession corresponds to FNSII-1 vs FNSII-2. Full text needed to map CYP93B24 to either FNSII-1 or FNSII-2 and confirm substrate. [UPDATED FROM FULLTEXT] CYP93B24 = SbFNSII-1 in Scutellaria baicalensis. Broad substrate specificity for flavanones (unlike SbFNSII-2/CYP93B25 which is pinocembrin-specific). SbFNSII-1 groups with CYP93B6 (Perilla frutescens) and CYP93B23 (O. basilicum) in phylogenetic tree. SbFNSII-1 contributes to 4-hydroxyflavone biosynthesis in aerial parts; root-specific pinocembrin->chrysin->baicalein pathway relies on SbFNSII-2. RNAi silencing of both FNSII isoforms used to confirm pathway assignment.

Same Sci Adv 2016 abstract as CYP93B24. Accession KT963454 is CYP93B25. Abstract discusses FNSII-1 and FNSII-2 but does not explicitly assign accessions to names. Full text needed to map CYP93B25 to FNSII-1 or FNSII-2. [UPDATED FROM FULLTEXT] CYP93B25 = SbFNSII-2, flavone synthase II specific for pinocembrin (4-deoxyflavanone) -> chrysin (4-deoxyflavone). Contrasts with SbFNSII-1 which has broad specificity for flavanones. Paper states FNSII-2 is specific for pinocembrin and is responsible for synthesis of 4-deoxyflavones such as chrysin and wogonin. Pinocembrin (4-deoxyflavanone) is converted by FNS to form chrysin (4-deoxyflavone) in the 4-deoxyflavone pathway of S. baicalensis roots.

reaction_type: flavanone to flavone direct conversion (flavone synthase II)
notes: Abstract explicitly states recombinant LjFNSII-1.1 (along with LjFNSII-2.1 and LmFNSII-1.1) converted eriodictyol, naringenin, and liquiritigenin to corresponding flavones directly in NADPH-dependent manner. Single amino acid at position 242 (Glu→Lys) causes catalytic differences between LjFNSII-1.1 and LjFNSII-2.1.

reaction_type: flavanone to flavone direct conversion (flavone synthase II)
notes: Same Sci Rep 2016 abstract. LjFNSII-2.1 explicitly named as converting same three flavanone substrates as LjFNSII-1.1. Reduced catalytic activity vs LjFNSII-1.1 due to single residue substitution at position 242.

reaction_type: flavanone to flavone direct conversion (flavone synthase II)
notes: Same Sci Rep 2016 abstract. LmFNSII-1.1 explicitly named as converting same three flavanone substrates to flavones directly. Weak catalytic activity and low gene expression in flowers account for low flavone accumulation in L. macranthoides.

Abstract identifies CYP93C1 (one of two soybean IFS genes identified) as isoflavone synthase. Expression in Arabidopsis produced genistein from naringenin. The abstract names naringenin → genistein conversion as the functional output of soybean IFS. This is the first identification of IFS in legumes.

First paper explicitly names CYP93C1v2: microsomes from insect cells convert liquiritigenin to daidzein (via 2,4',7-trihydroxyisoflavanone) and naringenin to genistein at lower rate. Second paper (JBC 2001) demonstrates CYP93C1v2 efficiently uses 6,7,4'-trihydroxyflavanone as substrate, producing 6,7,4'-trihydroxyisoflavone. Two substrates from two different papers; no conflict.

Abstract explicitly names CYP93C2 (CYP Ge-8) from licorice and demonstrates in yeast microsomes that liquiritigenin → daidzein and naringenin → genistein (both via 2-hydroxyisoflavanone intermediates). Chemical structures confirmed by mass spectrometry.

Same Nat Biotechnol 2000 paper as CYP93C1 (entry 479). Abstract describes two soybean IFS genes but does not name CYP93C5 explicitly. CYP93C5 as a second IFS paralog of soybean is likely the second gene mentioned, but the abstract does not differentiate accessions. Full text required.

substrates: flavanones (liquiritigenin, naringenin implied for IFS class)
notes: Abstract names LjCYP-1 (CYP93C family) as having 2-hydroxyisoflavanone synthase (IFS) activity when expressed in yeast. CYP93C17 is the systematic name for LjCYP-1. Specific substrate names not listed individually in abstract; inferred from IFS class activity (liquiritigenin/naringenin). Involved in vestitol biosynthesis pathway. [QC: plausible but not directly verified from abstract]

Title-only entry: 'Functional expression and subcellular localization of pea polymorphic isoflavone synthase CYP93C18'. No abstract available. Substrate cannot be determined from title alone, though IFS activity is suggested by the title.

substrates: flavanones (naringenin, liquiritigenin implied for IFS class)
notes: Abstract explicitly names CYP93C20 as isoflavone synthase (IFS) from M. truncatula and confirms the engineered soluble form has the same activity as the full-length membrane-associated enzyme in yeast. Specific substrates not named in abstract; IFS class activity implies liquiritigenin/naringenin as substrates.

reaction_type: 2-hydroxyisoflavanone synthase (inferred from accession in IFS paper)
notes: Accession AF195807 is listed as an isoflavone synthase homolog from mung bean (Vigna radiata) in the Nat Biotechnol 2000 paper. Abstract does not explicitly name or characterize AF195807. Functional confirmation requires full text.

reaction_type: 2-hydroxyisoflavanone synthase (inferred from accession in IFS paper)
notes: Accession AF195811 is listed as an IFS homolog from red clover (Trifolium pratense) in the Nat Biotechnol 2000 paper. Abstract does not explicitly characterize AF195811. Functional confirmation requires full text.

reaction_type: 2-hydroxyisoflavanone synthase (inferred from accession in IFS paper)
notes: Accession AF195812 is listed as an IFS homolog from pea (Pisum sativum) in the Nat Biotechnol 2000 paper. Abstract does not explicitly characterize AF195812. Functional confirmation requires full text.
No papers provided. Accession AY253284 given. Based on name (IFS = isoflavone synthase) and species (red clover), this is likely an isoflavone synthase, but no evidence in this entry to confirm.

Abstract explicitly states IFS2_12 expressed in tobacco (both transiently and stably) produced genistein and its conjugates, confirming IFS activity. Positive control (soybean IFS/alfalfa CHI) also produced genistein. Naringenin is the implied substrate (standard for IFS to genistein conversion) but not explicitly named in the abstract.

First paper (FEBS J 2006) explicitly names CYP93E1 and demonstrates hydroxylating activity on beta-amyrin (product: olean-12-ene-3beta,24-diol) and sophoradiol (product: soyasapogenol B) by GC-MS. Co-expression with beta-amyrin synthase in yeast confirmed in vivo activity. Second paper (Phytochem 2014) confirms CYP93E subfamily catalyzes C-24 oxidation of triterpene backbone.

Abstract explicitly states LjCYP93E1 converted beta-amyrin into 24-hydroxy-beta-amyrin (metabolic intermediate of soyasapogenols). In planta function confirmed by LORE1 insertional mutant: complete abolition of soyasapogenols and soyasaponin I in mutant plants.

First paper (Phytochem 2014) explicitly describes CYP93E2 catalyzing C-24 oxidation of beta-amyrin, though with poor in vivo efficiency in yeast. Second paper (PCP 2013) explicitly identifies CYP93E2 as key enzyme in non-hemolytic sapogenin pathway in M. truncatula, converting beta-amyrin to 24-OH-beta-amyrin. Consistent across two independent papers.

reaction_type: triterpene C-24 hydroxylation (inferred from CYP93E subfamily)
notes: Abstract is entirely about CYP88D6 (licorice beta-amyrin 11-oxidase), not CYP93E3. CYP93E3 (accession AB437320) is not mentioned in the abstract. The paper concerns glycyrrhizin biosynthesis and CYP88D6 specifically. CYP93E3 substrate must be confirmed from a different source or full text.

products: olean-12-ene-3beta,24-diol and/or 3beta-hydroxy olean-12-en-24-oic acid (C-24 oxidation products)
notes: Moses et al. 2014 abstract states all six CYP93E orthologs screened (including CYP93E4 from Arachis hypogaea, accession KF906535) catalyze C-24 oxidation of beta-amyrin in S. cerevisiae, though with varying efficiencies. CYP93E9 is highlighted as most active. CYP93E4 is confirmed functional but its specific efficiency is not stated individually.

products: C-24 oxidation products (olean-12-ene-3beta,24-diol and/or 3beta-hydroxy olean-12-en-24-oic acid)
notes: Same Moses et al. 2014 paper. CYP93E5 from Cicer arietinum (accession KF906536) confirmed as functional C-24 oxidase on beta-amyrin in yeast. Specific catalytic efficiency not stated individually in abstract.

products: C-24 oxidation products (olean-12-ene-3beta,24-diol and/or 3beta-hydroxy olean-12-en-24-oic acid)
notes: Same Moses et al. 2014 paper. CYP93E6 from Glycyrrhiza glabra (accession KF906537) confirmed functional C-24 oxidase in yeast. Specific catalytic efficiency not stated individually in abstract.

products: C-24 oxidation products (olean-12-ene-3beta,24-diol and/or 3beta-hydroxy olean-12-en-24-oic acid)
notes: Same Moses et al. 2014 paper. CYP93E7 from Lens culinaris (accession KF906538) confirmed functional C-24 oxidase in yeast. Specific catalytic efficiency not stated individually in abstract.

products: C-24 oxidation products (olean-12-ene-3beta,24-diol and/or 3beta-hydroxy olean-12-en-24-oic acid)
notes: Same Moses et al. 2014 paper. CYP93E8 from Pisum sativum (accession KF906539) confirmed functional C-24 oxidase in yeast. Specific catalytic efficiency not stated individually in abstract.

Abstract explicitly highlights CYP93E9 from Phaseolus vulgaris (accession KF906540) as showing highest activity among the screened orthologs, converting ~80% of in vivo produced beta-amyrin to olean-12-ene-3beta,24-diol and probable 3beta-hydroxy olean-12-en-24-oic acid. Catalytic efficiency 61x higher than M. truncatula CYP93E2.

Abstract explicitly states CYP93G1 desaturated naringenin → apigenin and eriodictyol → luteolin in recombinant enzyme assays. Confirmed in planta by transgenic Arabidopsis accumulating flavone O-glycosides. Rice cyp93g1 mutant shows preferential depletion of tricin O-linked flavanolignans and glycosides. Clearly distinguished from CYP93G2 (F2H) which makes 2-hydroxyflavanones.

Abstract explicitly states CYP93G2 (Os06g01250) converts naringenin and eriodictyol to corresponding 2-hydroxyflavanones in vitro (NADPH-dependent). Also generates 2-hydroxyflavanones for O-glycosylation in transgenic Arabidopsis. RNAi knockdown in rice depletes C-glycosylapigenin, C-glycosylluteolin, C-glycosylchrysoeriol. Conclusive in vitro and in vivo evidence.

Abstract explicitly names CYP93G3 (SbFNSII) as flavone synthase II in sorghum, confirmed by transgenic Arabidopsis expression. Metabolite analysis detected 2-hydroxynaringenin hexosides and 2-hydroxyeriodictyol hexosides in transgenic plants, indicating CYP93G3 catalyzes flavanone 2-hydroxylation (same mechanism as CYP93B subfamily). First FNSII characterized in a monocot.

Abstract is a genome-wide P1 transcription factor study in maize. It identifies F2H1 (a P450 converting naringenin to 2-hydroxynaringenin) but does not explicitly name CYP93G5. Database function field states 'Catalyzes 2-hydroxylation of naringenin and eriodictyol' but this is not stated in the abstract. Cannot confirm CYP93G5 = F2H1 from abstract alone. Full text required. [UPDATED FROM FULLTEXT] CYP93G5 = F2H1 (flavanone 2-hydroxylase 1) in maize. Function metadata: catalyzes 2-hydroxylation of naringenin and eriodictyol. Paper (Plant Cell 2012): F2H1 is a P450 enzyme that converts naringenin into 2-hydroxynaringenin, a key branch point in the P1-controlled pathway and first step in formation of insecticidal C-glycosyl flavones. Regulated by P1 (R2R3-MYB transcription factor) in maize silks and pericarps. [QC VERIFIED]

reaction_type: flavanone to flavone direct conversion (flavone synthase II)
notes: Abstract explicitly names ZmCYP93G7 (FNSII) as having flavone synthase activity and able to convert naringenin and eriodictyol into apigenin and luteolin respectively. Confirmed by complementation of Arabidopsis dmr6 mutant. Expression regulated by C1/PL1+R/B anthocyanin complexes and UV-B. ZmFNSII (CYP93G7) synthesizes apigenin conferring UV-B protection.

Abstract identifies a CYP93G subfamily member as a flavanone 2-hydroxylase, but does not distinguish which specific enzyme (CYP93G10 vs CYP93G15) is responsible. The function field assigns 'Flavone synthase II' to CYP93G10 (converting naringenin→apigenin, eriodictyol→luteolin), but this activity is not confirmed in the abstract text. Fulltext required to confirm CYP93G10-specific substrate. [UPDATED FROM FULLTEXT] CYP93G10 is a CYP93G subfamily flavanone 2-hydroxylase in maize. Paper (Plant Physiology 2021): a CYP in the CYP93G subfamily serves as flavanone 2-hydroxylase providing substrate for FOMT2-catalyzed formation of xilonenin. Products are 2-hydroxynaringenin-derived (xilonenin). Function metadata lists broader FNSII activity (naringenin->apigenin, eriodictyol->luteolin) which is inconsistent with paper text; paper text evidence (2-hydroxylation) is used here. The enzyme is induced by fungal infection and contributes to antifungal defense. [QC: plausible but not directly verified from abstract]

Abstract confirms 'a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase in the CYP93G subfamily was found to serve as a flavanone 2-hydroxylase providing the substrate for FOMT2-catalyzed formation of xilonenin.' Function field explicitly assigns this activity to CYP93G15 with substrates naringenin and eriodictyol. Products are 2-hydroxynaringenin-derived; xilonenin is the downstream end product. Confidence is medium rather than high because the abstract does not explicitly name CYP93G15 by name — attribution relies on function field combined with abstract context.

Three independent papers confirm CYP98A3 activity. Primary paper (Schoch 2001): very actively converted 5-O-shikimate ester of p-coumaric acid (4x faster than quinate ester); free p-coumaric acid and CoA/glucose esters were NOT metabolized. Second paper (Franke 2002): also accepts p-coumarate and other p-hydroxylated substrates. Third paper (Nair 2002): hydroxylates p-coumaric acid to caffeic acid in vivo in yeast (very slowly). Consensus: p-coumaroylshikimate is the primary substrate; p-coumaroylquinate is secondary; free p-coumaric acid is accepted at low activity.

Alber 2019 abstract states that in four angiosperm species tested, 4-coumaroyl-shikimate was the preferred substrate of one member in each species. Brachypodium distachyon is one of the four species, and CYP98A4 is the entry for this species. However, the abstract does not explicitly name CYP98A4 — individual enzyme names and kinetic data require fulltext access.

Abstract explicitly states CYP98A6 'catalyze the 3-hydroxylation of 4-coumaroyl-4'-hydroxyphenyllactic acid, one of the final two steps leading to rosmarinic acid.' Expressed in yeast and biochemically characterized. Reaction is part of rosmarinic acid biosynthesis in Lithospermum erythrorhizon.

Abstract describes two partially redundant P450s (CYP98A8 and CYP98A9) that catalyze a cascade of six successive hydroxylations leading to N1,N5-di(hydroxyferuloyl)-N10-sinapoylspermidine in pollen. The abstract does not specify which of the two P450s acts on which specific substrate, nor does it name the individual substrates at each step. Fulltext required to determine CYP98A8-specific substrates.

Same paper as CYP98A8 (entry 511). Two partially redundant P450s (CYP98A8 and CYP98A9) involved in hydroxylation cascade toward N1,N5-di(hydroxyferuloyl)-N10-sinapoylspermidine. Abstract does not specify individual substrate assignments for CYP98A9. Fulltext required.

Morant 2007 abstract describes eight wheat CYP98s; three of the eight have phenol meta-hydroxylase activity with p-coumaroylshikimate as primary substrate. CYP98A10 is one of the eight, but the abstract does not specify which three are active. Fulltext required to confirm whether CYP98A10 is among the active three.
Same paper as CYP98A10 (entry 513). One of eight wheat CYP98s; only three showed activity in the study. Abstract does not specify whether CYP98A11 is among the active enzymes. Fulltext required.
Same paper as CYP98A10 and CYP98A11. One of eight wheat CYP98s; three showed activity. Abstract does not identify CYP98A12 specifically as active or inactive. Fulltext required.

Abstract explicitly states: 'Two basil cDNAs encoding isozymes of cytochrome P450 CYP98A13, which meta hydroxylates p-coumaroyl shikimate, were isolated... the basil enzymes were found to be very specific for p-coumaroyl shikimate.' Both isozymes (CYP98A13v1 and CYP98A13v2) show high specificity for p-coumaroylshikimate.

Same paper as CYP98A13v1 (entry 516). Both isozymes (v1 and v2, 90% amino acid identity) show high specificity for p-coumaroylshikimate. Abstract explicitly confirms: 'the basil enzymes were found to be very specific for p-coumaroyl shikimate.'

Abstract explicitly states: 'CYP98A14 protein catalysed the 3-hydroxylation of 4-coumaroyl-3',4'-dihydroxyphenyllactate (Km 5 μM) and the 3'-hydroxylation of caffeoyl-4'-hydroxyphenyllactate (Km 40 μM), in both cases forming rosmarinic acid.' CYP98A14 does NOT accept 4-coumaroylshikimate or 4-coumaroylquinate. Novel bifunctional P450 specialized for rosmarinic acid biosynthesis in Coleus blumei.

Alber 2019 abstract explicitly states: 'The gymnosperm CYP98 from Pinus taeda showed a broad substrate range, but preferred 4-coumaroyl-shikimate as its best substrate.' CYP98A19 is the Pinus taeda entry. Broad substrate range implies additional substrates accepted; specific secondary substrates require fulltext.

Abstract explicitly states CYP98A22 'adds a 3-OH to p-coumaroyl ester derivatives but is more efficient to convert p-coumaroyl quinate into chlorogenic acid than to metabolize p-coumaroyl shikimate.' Primary substrate is p-coumaroylquinate (→ chlorogenic acid); secondary substrate is p-coumaroylshikimate. Expressed in Nicotiana benthamiana heterologous system.

Alber 2019 abstract states Populus trichocarpa has independent duplicates with broad substrate ranges, accepting numerous 4-coumaroyl-esters and -amines. However, the abstract does not distinguish which specific Populus paralog (CYP98A23 vs CYP98A27) shows the broad range versus shikimate preference. Fulltext required to assign substrates specifically to CYP98A23.

Coleman 2008 (PNAS) explicitly characterizes C3'H in hybrid poplar (CYP98A27): 'C3'H... catalyzes the 3'-hydroxylation of p-coumaroyl shikimate and p-coumaroyl quinate.' RNAi suppression confirmed in planta accumulation of p-coumaroyl shikimate. The 2019 Alber paper provides additional context (broad substrate range for Populus paralogs). Confidence high for p-coumaroylshikimate and p-coumaroylquinate from 2008 paper.

Alber 2019 abstract explicitly names CYP98A34: 'The best substrate for CYP98A34 from the moss Physcomitrella patens was also 4-coumaroyl-anthranilate, while 4-coumaroyl-shikimate was converted to lower extents.' Primary substrate: 4-coumaroyl-anthranilate; secondary: 4-coumaroylshikimate. Note that despite in vitro activity with 4-coumaroyl-shikimate, CYP98A34 could not complement the Arabidopsis cyp98a3 loss-of-function phenotype. The 2017 Nat Commun paper (Renault) characterizes function in vivo but does not state substrates in the abstract.

Mahesh 2007 abstract explicitly states: 'CYP98A35 appears to be the first C3'H capable of metabolising p-coumaroyl quinate and p-coumaroyl shikimate with the same efficiency.' Both substrates converted in yeast expression system. CYP98A35 is distinguished from CYP98A36 by its ability to also convert p-coumaroylquinate.

Mahesh 2007 abstract explicitly states: 'both [CYP98A35 and CYP98A36] metabolized p-coumaroyl shikimate at similar rates, but that only one [CYP98A35] hydroxylates the chlorogenic acid precursor p-coumaroyl quinate.' CYP98A36 therefore converts p-coumaroylshikimate but NOT p-coumaroylquinate (unlike CYP98A35).

Alber 2019 abstract states: 'CYP98s from the lycophyte Selaginella moellendorffii... were able to use alternative substrates, in particular 4-coumaroyl-anthranilate' and 'converted 4-coumaroyl-shikimate poorly in vitro.' CYP98A38 is the Selaginella entry. Primary substrate is 4-coumaroyl-anthranilate; 4-coumaroylshikimate is a poor substrate. Fulltext would confirm whether CYP98A38 is the specific accession characterized.

Sullivan 2010 abstract explicitly states: 'CYP98A44 expressed in Saccharomyces cerevisiae is capable of hydroxylating p-coumaroyl-shikimate, but not p-coumaroyl-malate.' Substrate p-coumaroylshikimate confirmed; p-coumaroyl-malate explicitly excluded. This finding indicates phaselic acid biosynthesis in red clover proceeds via caffeoyl transfer to malic acid rather than via hydroxylation of p-coumaroyl-malate.

Moglia 2009 abstract states that CYP98A49 was 'heterologously expressed in yeast, in order to perform an enzymatic assay with p-coumaroylshikimate and p-coumaroylquinate as substrates.' The abstract confirms the assay was performed but does not state which substrates were converted or the kinetic results. Fulltext required to confirm enzymatic activity and substrate preference.

The cited paper (Marques 2013) characterizes CYP719A23 and CYP719A24 in podophyllotoxin biosynthesis — these are completely different P450 families from CYP98A68. CYP98A68 is mentioned in the database entry but is not the subject of the cited paper. No substrate information for CYP98A68 can be extracted from this abstract. A different publication may be needed.

Alber 2019 abstract states Amborella trichopoda has independent duplicates with broad substrate ranges, accepting numerous 4-coumaroyl-esters and -amines. However, Amborella has two entries (CYP98A84 and CYP98A85), and the abstract does not specify which has broad vs. preferred shikimate activity. Fulltext required to assign substrates specifically to CYP98A84.

Same paper and same limitation as CYP98A84 (entry 530). Amborella has two CYP98 paralogs, one with broad substrate range and one with shikimate preference. Abstract does not resolve which paralog is CYP98A85. Fulltext required.

Alber 2019 abstract states: 'CYP98s from the... fern Pteris vittata converted 4-coumaroyl-shikimate poorly in vitro, but were able to use alternative substrates, in particular 4-coumaroyl-anthranilate.' CYP98A104 is the Pteris vittata entry. Preferred substrate: 4-coumaroyl-anthranilate. 4-coumaroylshikimate is a poor substrate, suggesting caffeoyl-shikimate is unlikely to be a monolignol biosynthesis intermediate in ferns.

Levsh 2019 abstract describes rosmarinic acid biosynthesis in P. campanularia involving 'a BAHD acyltransferase and two cytochrome P450 hydroxylases.' Three CYP98A entries from this paper (CYP98A111, CYP98A112, CYP98A113) are in the database. The abstract does not name specific substrates for individual P450s, nor does it specify which of the three accessions corresponds to the two active hydroxylases. Fulltext required. reaction_type: aromatic 3-hydroxylation (3'-hydroxylation, as part of membrane complex)
notes: Chen 2011 (PNAS) explicitly characterizes PtrC3H3 by name: 'two cinnamic acid 4-hydroxylases (PtrC4H1 and PtrC4H2) and a p-coumaroyl ester 3-hydroxylase (PtrC3H3).' Two 3-hydroxylation paths identified: (1) p-coumaric acid → caffeic acid and (2) p-coumaroyl shikimic acid → caffeoyl shikimic acid. Activity is greatly enhanced in membrane protein complexes (PtrC4H1/C4H2/C3H3, 70-6500x higher efficiency than individual proteins). Reaction confirmed both in yeast recombinant and in planta.

First paper: CYP701A1 cDNA 'encodes an ent-kaurene oxidase activity' confirmed by complementation of Arabidopsis ga3-2 mutant. Second paper cited is about CYP88A (ent-kaurenoic acid oxidase, a different enzyme) and does not add substrate information for CYP701A1. Substrate ent-kaurene, product ent-kaurenoic acid (via three sequential oxidation steps: ent-kaurene → ent-kaurenol → ent-kaurenal → ent-kaurenoic acid, by analogy with CYP701A3). [QC VERIFIED]

Three papers confirm CYP701A3 activity. Helliwell 1999: GA3 (CYP701A3) catalyzes three steps from ent-kaurene to ent-kaurenoic acid. Morrone 2010: detailed mechanism — three hydroxylations via ent-kaurenol and ent-kaurenal intermediates, with gem-diol dehydration; ent-beyerene only hydroxylated once (not full oxidation), indicating requirement for exact kaurane ring structure. Mafu 2016: promiscuity study with >20 diterpene substrates tested (structural details require fulltext). Primary substrate is ent-kaurene; additional labdane-related diterpenes accepted with reduced efficiency.

Two papers confirm CYP701A5 (SrKO) as kaurene oxidase in Stevia. Humphrey 2006: KO is in the GA biosynthetic pathway branch, converts (-)-kaurene to (-)-kaurenoic acid; subcellular location confirmed at ER. Gold 2018: SrKO (CYP701A5) confirmed in steviol glucoside production pathway from kaurene. SrKO was outperformed by novel KO75 in yeast assays but its activity is well established. Substrate: ent-kaurene; product: ent-kaurenoic acid (precursor to steviol via CYP701A5 then kaurenoic acid hydroxylase).

Three papers confirm CYP701A6 (OsKO2) as ent-kaurene oxidase in rice GA biosynthesis. Ko 2008: 'microsomes from Pichia pastoris expressing OsKO2 converted ent-kaurene to ent-kaurenoic acid' — direct biochemical evidence. Wang 2012: confirms CYP701A6 = OsKO2 for GA biosynthesis (only one of five rice CYP701A members required for GA). Mafu 2016: promiscuity study (additional substrates tested). Substrate: ent-kaurene; product: ent-kaurenoic acid.

reaction_type: C-3 hydroxylation of labdane-related diterpenes (specialized metabolism)
notes: CYP701A8 (OsKOL4) is functionally divergent from canonical ent-kaurene oxidases. Wang 2012: 'OsKOL4 instead efficiently reacts with ent-sandaracopimaradiene and ent-cassadiene to produce the corresponding C3alpha-hydroxylated diterpenoids' (oryzalexin and phytocassane precursors). Wu 2013: confirms CYP701A8 C-3alpha hydroxylation; poor activity on 7beta-hydroxy-ent-sandaracopimaradiene. Kitaoka 2015: CYP701A8 also catalyzes 3beta-hydroxylation of syn-pimaradiene (relevant to momilactone biosynthesis). De La Peña 2021: momilactone pathway context. CYP701A8 does NOT catalyze canonical ent-kaurene→ent-kaurenoic acid conversion.

Mao 2017 abstract explicitly states: 'CYP701A26, which reacted with ent-kaurene to form ent-kaurenoic acid, the key intermediate of GA biosynthesis.' Also noted: 'CYP701A26 exhibited substrate promiscuity to catalyze oxidation of other labdane related diterpenes.' Primary substrate ent-kaurene confirmed; secondary substrates (other labdane diterpenes) require fulltext for specifics. Note: CYP701A43 (a maize homolog) showed no activity on ent-kaurene or other tested substrates.

Su 2016 abstract explicitly states: 'SmKO catalyzes the three-step oxidation of ent-kaurene to ent-kaurenoic acid.' Confirmed by yeast expression system. Part of the gibberellin biosynthetic pathway in Salvia miltiorrhiza (GA pathway from GGPP to ent-kaurenoic acid clarified). Note: Salvia miltiorrhiza also has a separate tanshinone diterpenoid pathway; SmKO is specifically for the GA branch.

Su 2017 abstract explicitly states: 'TwKO catalyzed the three-step oxidation of the C4alpha methyl of ent-kaurene to form ent-kaurenoic acid as an early step in GA biosynthesis.' Additionally: 'TwKO could also convert 16alpha-hydroxy-ent-kaurane to 16alpha-hydroxy-ent-kaurenoic acid.' The second activity is implicated in the tripterifordin (anti-HIV principle) biosynthetic pathway. Molecular docking identified Leu387 as a key residue for the second substrate specificity.

Davidson 2004 abstract explicitly states: 'PsKO1 has ent-kaurene oxidase (KO) activity, catalyzing the three step oxidation of ent-kaurene to ent-kaurenoic acid in the gibberellin (GA) biosynthetic pathway when expressed in yeast.' PsKO1 is encoded by the LH gene; three independent lh mutant alleles confirmed — lh-1 allele failed to metabolize ent-kaurene in yeast. Single-copy gene expressed in all tissues (stems, roots, seeds).

Sawada 2008 abstract states: 'Using a Pichia pastoris system, it was found that LsKO1 and LsKO2 encode ent-kaurene oxidases.' Both are confirmed by functional assay. Activity (ent-kaurene → ent-kaurenoic acid) inferred from ent-kaurene oxidase designation. Individual kinetic parameters for LsKO1 vs LsKO2 not differentiated in the abstract; both confirmed functional.

Same paper as LsKO1 (entry 546). Both LsKO1 and LsKO2 confirmed as ent-kaurene oxidases by Pichia pastoris functional assay (Sawada 2008). No individual kinetic differentiation provided in the abstract.

Gold 2018 abstract describes KO75 (CYP701 family) as a novel kaurene oxidase that converts kaurene to kaurenoic acid in steviol glucoside production. KO75 outperformed SrKO (CYP701A5) in yeast assays. Species of origin is listed as 'na' (unknown/not assigned) in the database entry. Activity is confirmed in recombinant yeast system with supplemented kaurene substrate. Confidence is medium because species identity is unknown and fulltext would confirm exact substrate stereospecificity.

Miyazaki 2011 abstract explicitly states: 'The recombinant CYP701B1 protein catalyzed the oxidation reaction from ent-kaurene to ent-kaurenoic acid.' Confirmed in yeast heterologous expression. Notable property: CYP701B1 is highly resistant to the ent-kaurene oxidase inhibitor uniconazole-P (IC50 64 μM) compared to Arabidopsis CYP701A3 (IC50 0.26 μM), suggesting distinct active site architecture despite same substrate.

Imaishi 1999 abstract states: 'The recombinant yeast microsomes containing the CYP703A1 hemoprotein were found to metabolize lauric acid.' Substrate lauric acid confirmed; specific hydroxylation position not stated in the abstract (contrast with CYP703A2 where C-7 is specified). By analogy with the well-characterized CYP703A2, in-chain hydroxylation is expected. Expression restricted to early floral bud stage. Confidence is medium because exact hydroxylation site requires fulltext.

reaction_type: fatty acid in-chain hydroxylation (C-7 position preferred)
notes: Morant 2007 abstract explicitly states: 'CYP703 catalyzes the conversion of medium-chain saturated fatty acids to the corresponding monohydroxylated fatty acids, with a preferential hydroxylation of lauric acid at the C-7 position.' In planta confirmation: 'lauric acid and in-chain hydroxy lauric acids are the in planta substrate and product, respectively.' CYP703A2 knockout shows impaired pollen wall development with absent exine. Products (hydroxy lauric acids) are essential building blocks for sporopollenin synthesis in pollen.

substrates: primary oxidation products of CYP706A3 itself
notes: Abstract explicitly states CYP706A3 is active on TPS11 sesquiterpene products and further oxidizes its own primary oxidation products. Coexpression with TPS11 suppresses sesquiterpene and most monoterpene volatile emission. Specific individual sesquiterpene substrate names not listed in abstract; requires fulltext for precise substrate identities. Promiscuous enzyme.

Abstract explicitly states CYP706B1 catalyzes hydroxylation of (+)-delta-cadinene to 8-hydroxy-(+)-delta-cadinene. Characterized by heterologous expression in yeast. First CYP706 family member with determined function. Early step in gossypol biosynthesis.

Abstract explicitly states carlactone is the substrate: 'derived from carlactone as substrate.' OsCYP706C2 acts with two methyltransferases to produce 4-oxo-MeCLA. The function field mentions 4-oxo-19-OH-carlactone as an intermediate. 4-oxo-MeCLA is the inaugural noncanonical strigolactone identified in rice root exudate.

Abstract explicitly states ZmCYP706C37 catalyzes a series of oxidative steps in maize strigolactone biosynthesis. Function field specifies methyl carlactonoate → zealactone and carlactone → zealactol. Abstract names zealactol and zealactonoic acid as strigolactones with reduced Striga germination activity.

Abstract explicitly states CYP706C55 catalyzes the dehydration of phenylacetaldoxime, an unusual cytochrome P450 reaction. Product is phenylacetonitrile, which is subsequently hydroxylated by CYP71B103 to form mandelonitrile. Part of a unique prunasin biosynthetic enzyme configuration in E. cladocalyx.

Abstract explicitly states CYP706M1 (CnVO, C. nootkatensis valencene oxidase) produces trans-nootkatol and (+)-nootkatone upon co-expression with valencene synthase in yeast. (+)-nootkatone detected at 144±10 μg/L. This is the founding member of the CYP706M subfamily.

Abstract explicitly states IrCYP706V2 oxidizes the ent-kaurene core in the initial stage of oridonin biosynthesis. The specific hydroxylation position (7β) is from the function field, not the abstract. Abstract confirms ent-kaurene as substrate for V2 specifically (named alongside V7). Confidence medium because the 7β regiochemistry requires fulltext for verification.

Abstract describes engineering yeast for breviscapine production and identifies 'flavone-6-hydroxylase' as one of two key enzymes from E. breviscapus genome. EbCYP706X is not referenced by this name in the abstract. The specific substrate (likely apigenin or a related flavone) is not stated in the abstract. Requires fulltext to confirm identity and substrate of EbCYP706X as the flavone-6-hydroxylase. [UPDATED FROM FULLTEXT] EbCYP706X = F6H (flavone-6-hydroxylase) in Erigeron breviscapus. Paper (Nat Commun 2018): F6H converts apigenin -> scutellarein by 6-hydroxylation; works together with F7GAT (flavonoid-7-O-glucuronosyltransferase) to produce scutellarin from apigenin. F6H is an Asteraceae-specific CYP706 family enzyme. Also stated to hydroxylate apigenin-7-O-glucuronide at position 6 as alternative route to scutellarin. Two major products of breviscapine pathway: scutellarin (108 mg/L) and apigenin-7-O-glucuronide (185 mg/L) in engineered yeast.

Abstract explicitly states CYP712G1 catalyzes the double oxidation of orobanchol resulting in formation of three didehydro-orobanchol (DDH) isomers. One DDH isomer is further converted to solanacol. Abstract also suggests hydroxy-orobanchol is the likely intermediate. Functional characterization by heterologous expression in N. benthamiana and yeast.

Abstract explicitly states CYP712K1 (along with K2 and K3) effectively oxidizes friedelin to form 29-hydroxy-friedelin and polpunonic acid. CYP712K1 was specifically expanded in yeast platform to produce polpunonic acid at 1.4 mg/L. All three P450s act on friedelin; C-29 oxidation specificity stated in function field. Also noted: CYP712K2 and CYP712K3 have same reported activity.

Abstract explicitly groups CYP712K1, CYP712K2, and CYP712K3 as acting on friedelin to form 29-hydroxy-friedelin and polpunonic acid. Individual kinetic distinction between K1/K2/K3 requires fulltext. Substrate friedelin is explicit.

Abstract explicitly groups CYP712K1, CYP712K2, and CYP712K3 as acting on friedelin to form 29-hydroxy-friedelin and polpunonic acid. Individual kinetic distinction between K1/K2/K3 requires fulltext. Substrate friedelin is explicit.

Abstract explicitly states CYP712K4 catalyzes the oxidation of friedelin at the C-29 position leading to maytenoic acid via a three-step oxidation. Confirmed by heterologous expression in N. benthamiana and S. cerevisiae. Product structure confirmed by HRMS and NMR. Maytenoic acid = polpunonic acid (same compound, different names in different species contexts).

Abstract discusses genome mining characterizing three Arabidopsis cytochrome P450s and mentions P450 oxidation of thalianol, arabidiol, and marneral. However, the abstract does not individually assign CYP705A1 to a specific substrate. The accession At4g15330 links it to the thalianol cluster. Requires fulltext to confirm which specific triterpene is the substrate of CYP705A1.

Abstract describes the thalianol operon-like gene cluster in Arabidopsis required for triterpene synthesis. CYP705A5 is part of this cluster but is not individually named in the abstract with a specific substrate. Requires fulltext to identify the specific substrate of CYP705A5.

Abstract characterizes the marneral operon-like gene cluster in Arabidopsis. CYP705A12 is likely part of this cluster but is not individually named with a specific substrate in the abstract. Requires fulltext to confirm substrate. [PARTIAL FROM FULLTEXT] Paper (PNAS 2011) characterizes the marneral gene cluster in Arabidopsis thaliana. CYP705A12 is part of this operon-like triterpene gene cluster (marneral cluster). Paper text is truncated (abstract only, 3465 chars). Specific substrate of CYP705A12 cannot be confirmed from available text. From literature context, CYP705A12 is known to catalyze oxidation of marnerol (a marneral-derived triterpene alcohol) within the marneral cluster. Compound class not in metadata.

2003 JBC paper explicitly states CYP719A1 (canadine synthase) catalyzes conversion of (S)-tetrahydrocolumbamine to (S)-tetrahydroberberine. High substrate affinity and specificity for (S)-THC confirmed. (S)-scoulerine is explicitly NOT a substrate. The 2016 Narcross ACS Synth Biol paper is a general enzyme screening paper and does not provide individual substrate data for CYP719A1. Best evidence from 2003 paper.

2007 FEBS J paper explicitly states CYP719A2 had stylopine synthase activity from cheilanthifoline to stylopine. Enzymatic analysis showed CYP719A2 had high substrate affinity ONLY toward (R,S)-cheilanthifoline; (S)-scoulerine and (S)-tetrahydrocolumbamine were not high-affinity substrates for A2 (in contrast to A3). The 2016 Narcross paper is a general screen. Strict substrate specificity for cheilanthifoline.

reaction_type: methylenedioxy bridge formation (stylopine synthase, broad specificity)
notes: 2007 FEBS J paper explicitly states CYP719A3 had high affinity toward three substrates: (R,S)-cheilanthifoline, (S)-scoulerine, and (S)-tetrahydrocolumbamine. Both CYP719A2 and CYP719A3 catalyze methylenedioxy bridge formation from cheilanthifoline to stylopine. CYP719A3 has broader specificity than CYP719A2. Root-specific expression noted.

2009 Plant Cell Rep paper explicitly states CYP719A5 had cheilanthifoline synthase activity (scoulerine → cheilanthifoline), confirmed by enzyme assay of recombinant protein expressed in yeast. The 2016 Narcross paper is a general screen. Note: CYP719A9 from the same paper has activity toward (R,S)-reticuline (different substrate, different entry).

Only paper is the Narcross 2016 ACS Synth Biol screening paper. This paper describes a high-throughput screen of CYP719A subfamily homologues to reduce side-product synthesis but does not explicitly name CYP719A6's substrate in the abstract. Requires fulltext to determine substrate specificity.
Only paper is the Narcross 2016 ACS Synth Biol screening paper. Abstract does not explicitly name CYP719A7's substrate. Requires fulltext.

2009 Plant Cell Rep paper explicitly states enzyme assay of recombinant CYP719A9 suggested methylenedioxy bridge-forming activity toward (R,S)-reticuline. Abstract uses the word 'suggested,' indicating preliminary evidence. Expression in leaf correlates with pavine-type alkaloids. Confidence medium due to 'suggested' qualifier in abstract. Product structure not explicitly stated in abstract (methylenedioxy bridge-containing BIA). The 2016 Narcross paper is a general screen and does not add substrate information.

2011 ABB paper explicitly states CYP719A13 converts: (S)-tetrahydrocolumbamine → (S)-canadine (Km 2.7, kcat/Km 12.8, primary activity), (S)-cheilanthifoline → (S)-stylopine (Km 5.2, kcat/Km 2.6), (S)-scoulerine → (S)-nandinine (Km 8.1, kcat/Km 0.7). Twenty-seven substrates tested; these three are accepted. CYP719A13 can participate in both sanguinarine and berberine biosynthesis. The 2016 Narcross paper is a general screen.

2011 ABB paper explicitly states CYP719A14 transformed ONLY (S)-scoulerine to (S)-cheilanthifoline (Km 1.9±0.3, kcat/Km 1.7). Twenty-seven potential substrates tested; strict substrate specificity. Participates only in sanguinarine biosynthesis. The 2016 Narcross paper is a general screen.

Fossati 2014 Nat Commun paper reconstitutes a 10-gene pathway for dihydrosanguinarine from (R,S)-norlaudanosoline. CYP719A20 is part of this pathway but its specific substrate is not individually named in the abstract. The abstract focuses on the overall pathway reconstitution. The 2016 Narcross paper is a general screen. Requires fulltext to determine the specific methylenedioxy bridge substrate for CYP719A20.

2014 FEBS Lett paper explicitly states CYP719A21 converts (S)-tetrahydrocolumbamine to (S)-canadine with strict substrate specificity and high affinity (Km=4.63±0.71 μM). Virus-induced gene silencing confirmed in vivo role. Involved in noscapine biosynthesis in opium poppy.

2013 JBC paper explicitly states CYP719A23 (from P. hexandrum) converts (-)-matairesinol into (-)-pluviatolide by catalyzing methylenedioxy bridge formation. Other possible substrates tested but not accepted. The 2015 Science paper (Lau and Sattely) reconstitutes 10 genes for etoposide aglycone but does not provide new substrate data for CYP719A23 specifically in its abstract.

2013 JBC paper explicitly states CYP719A24 (from P. peltatum) converts (-)-matairesinol into (-)-pluviatolide by catalyzing methylenedioxy bridge formation, and did not act on other possible substrates tested. Highly similar to CYP719A23 from P. hexandrum with identical substrate.

Fossati 2014 Nat Commun paper reconstitutes the 10-gene dihydrosanguinarine pathway. CYP719A25 is part of the pathway but its individual substrate is not named in the abstract. The 2016 Narcross paper is a general screen. Requires fulltext to identify specific substrate.

The Pluskal 2019 Nat Plants paper elucidates kavalactone and flavokavain biosynthesis in kava. The abstract focuses on styrylpyrone synthases and a kavalactone reductase. CYP719A26 is not named in the abstract, and no substrate for this P450 is described. The connection between this paper and CYP719A26 is unclear from the abstract alone. Requires fulltext.

Abstract explicitly states methylenedioxy bridge formation was only detected when feruperic acid was used as substrate, and the product was identified as piperic acid. Two alternative precursors tested (ferulic acid and feruperine) were not accepted. Functionally expressed in yeast and characterized with a series of aromatic precursors. Involved in piperine biosynthesis in black pepper.

2023 Microb Cell Fact paper characterizes five CyCYP719A candidates from C. yanhusuo but explicitly names only CyCYP719A39 and CyCYP719A42 as having high catalytic efficiency. CYP719A38 is among the five candidates but is not individually described in the abstract. Function field states D ring methylenedioxy bridge formation on (S)-scoulerine and (S)-nandinine, but this is not confirmed by the abstract text. Requires fulltext. Abstract states the yeast strain with CyCYP719A39 starting from (S)-scoulerine produces (S)-stylopine. Paper text truncated before CYP867E38-specific characterization. CYP7005C1/C3 are characterized as oxygenating levopimaradiene -> ginkgosinoic acid A (compound 7, C20H30O2). For the remaining three CYPs including CYP867E38, the paper states only CYP7005C2 showed minor activity; CYP867E38 specific product not determinable from available text. Compound class: Diterpene.

Multiple papers discuss CYP72C1/SOB7 as a brassinosteroid-inactivating enzyme. Thornton et al. 2010 (Plant Mol Biol): CYP72C1 binds precursors of brassinolide/castasterone more effectively than the active BRs themselves, suggesting it acts on precursors rather than brassinolide. Turk et al. 2005: overexpression dramatically reduces castasterone. Nakamura et al. 2005 and Takahashi et al. 2005 show altered BR levels. The exact biochemical substrate has not been confirmed by direct enzyme assay in the abstract; the 2010 paper explicitly states 'the biochemical activity of CYP72C1 is unknown' and CYP72C1 has atypical active site. conflicting=true because papers indicate both precursor and castasterone are affected but direct substrate not confirmed.

It outperforms SrKAH (CYP81) from Stevia rebaudiana. KAH enzymes are known to convert ent-kaurenoic acid to steviol via 13-hydroxylation. Species is listed as 'na' (unknown); the functional substrate inference is based on the KAH functional class, not a direct substrate naming in the abstract. Confidence medium because substrate is inferred from functional class designation rather than explicit substrate assay result. [QC: plausible but not directly verified from abstract]

substrates: C12-C18 fatty acids (varying chain length and unsaturation)
products: omega-1 and omega-2 hydroxylated fatty acids
notes: Kandel et al. 2005 (J Biol Chem): CYP709C1 characterized by heterologous expression in yeast. Catalyzes omega-1 and omega-2 hydroxylation of C12-C18 fatty acids. Preferred substrate: cis-9,10-epoxystearic acid (Km 8 microM, Vmax 328 nmol/min/nmol P450). This compound is physiologically relevant as wheat microsomal peroxygenase can synthesize it from oleic acid. Methyl jasmonate treatment induces CYP709C1 expression 15-fold.

Nomura et al. 2013 (Plant Cell Physiol): recombinant CYP714A1 protein expressed in yeast catalyzes conversion of GA12 to 16-carboxy-16beta,17-dihydro GA12, a previously unidentified GA metabolite. Bioassays confirmed it is a GA inactivation enzyme. Overexpressing plants show extreme GA-deficient dwarf phenotype.

Nomura et al. 2013 (Plant Cell Physiol): recombinant CYP714A2 expressed in yeast converts ent-kaurenoic acid to steviol and converts GA12 to 12alpha-hydroxy GA12 (GA111, major product) and 13-hydroxy GA12 (GA53, minor). Multiple substrates confirmed. Transgenic overexpression confirms GA depletion phenotype. No conflicting data.

Magome et al. 2013 (PNAS): recombinant CYP714B1 expressed in yeast or insect cells converts GA12 into GA53 (13-OH GA12) in vitro. Rice cyp714b1 cyp714b2 double mutant has decreased 13-OH GAs and increased 13-H GAs. GA13-hydroxylase function confirmed by genetic and biochemical evidence.

Same paper as CYP714B1 (Magome et al. 2013): recombinant CYP714B2 also converts GA12 into GA53 in vitro. Functionally redundant with CYP714B1 in rice; double mutant phenotype confirms both genes play predominant role in GA 13-hydroxylation.

Zhu et al. 2006 (Plant Cell): heterologous expression in yeast showed EUI/CYP714D1 catalyzes 16alpha,17-epoxidation of non-13-hydroxylated GAs (GA4 explicitly mentioned). This epoxidation reduces biological activity of GA4. eui mutant accumulates large amounts of active GAs in the uppermost internode. Loss-of-function causes elongation; overexpression causes dwarfism. GA deactivation function firmly established.

CYP734A1 is the same gene as CYP72B1/BAS1. The 1999 paper (PNAS) identified the gene and showed accumulation of 26-hydroxybrassinolide in feeding experiments but did not directly establish biochemical function. The 2003 paper (Plant Physiol) expressed CYP72B1 in yeast and directly demonstrated C-26 hydroxylation of brassinolide and castasterone. Both papers are consistent; 2003 paper is the definitive biochemical characterization. Substrates extracted from the 2003 abstract.

In vitro assay confirmed CYP734A7 metabolizes castasterone to 26-hydroxycastasterone. Type I substrate-binding spectra Kd values: castasterone 6.7 µM, brassinolide 12 µM, 6-deoxocastasterone 12 µM. 28-norcastasterone also converted to hydroxylated product. All substrates explicitly stated in abstract.
